The deck's own objectives: explain mechanisms of non-β-lactam antimicrobials, identify antimicrobial adverse drug reactions, and design a regimen using patient risk factors plus spectrum of activity.
Scope note: despite the official wording “non-cell-wall,” this live deck begins with several non-β-lactam cell-wall and membrane agents (vancomycin, daptomycin, fosfomycin, polymyxins). They are included because they are explicitly taught in the current deck.

1. Cell-Wall + Cell-Membrane Active Agents

Vancomycin

MOA: binds D-Ala–D-Ala and inhibits trans-glycosidation/polymerization → cell lysis.

Spectrum: Gram-positive only; deck names S. aureus, Streptococcus, most Enterococcus, and Corynebacterium.

ADE/monitoring: nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, vancomycin-infusion syndrome; narrow therapeutic index requiring drug monitoring; vanA/B resistance.

Daptomycin

MOA: lipid tail anchors in the membrane; Ca²⁺-dependent pore/cation-channel formation → K⁺ loss → rapid depolarization.

Spectrum: Gram-positive organisms including Staph, Strep, Enterococcus, Corynebacterium.

ADE/pearls: rhabdomyolysis → weekly CPK; eosinophilic pneumonia; DRESS; inactivated by lung surfactant; low CNS levels.

Deck p. 5: Vancomycin summary integrates D-Ala–D-Ala targeting, Gram-positive spectrum, nephro/ototoxicity, infusion syndrome, vanA/B resistance, and therapeutic monitoring.
Deck p. 8: Daptomycin summary pairs membrane depolarization with Gram-positive coverage, weekly CPK for rhabdomyolysis, eosinophilic pneumonia/DRESS, and the lung-surfactant limitation.

Dalbavancin

Vancomycin-like spectrum; half-life 346 h (~2 weeks). Deck frames it as an emerging option for patients with barriers to standard care / bridge to discharge.

Oritavancin

Daptomycin-like spectrum; half-life 245 h (~10 days). Deck notes interaction with heparin anti-Xa labs.

Fosfomycin

Inactivates pyruvyl transferase → inhibits cell-wall synthesis. Most effective vs E. coli; also active against other Enterobacterales and E. faecalis. PO formulation = UTI use only.

Polymyxins

Rarely used; large molecules with a “detergent-like” mechanism: bind phospholipids → membrane leakage. Polymyxin B has better systemic absorption and may be less nephrotoxic. Colistin is excreted in urine and is associated with neurotoxicity + nephrotoxicity.

Fast trap: daptomycin can look attractive for severe Gram-positive pneumonia, but the deck explicitly says it is inactivated by lung surfactant.

2. DNA-Active Antibiotics

Fluoroquinolones

Topoisomerase II (DNA gyrase) and/or IV inhibition → impaired relaxation of supercoiled DNA + promotion of double-stranded DNA cleavage.
DrugDeck spectrum / clueMajor limitation
CiprofloxacinEnterobacterales + PseudomonasPoor Gram-positive coverage; not a respiratory FQ
LevofloxacinEnterobacterales + Pseudomonas + StrepLong t½ → once-daily dosing
MoxifloxacinEnterobacterales + Strep + anaerobesNo Pseudomonas; no urinary penetration
DelafloxacinEnterobacterales + Pseudomonas + Gram-positive (MRSA) + anaerobesExpensive; limited clinical data in deck
Deck p. 14: The deck compares ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, and delafloxacin side-by-side by spectrum and practical limitations.

Black-box / major warnings

Tendinitis/tendon rupture · myasthenia gravis exacerbation · peripheral neuropathy · muscle/joint/nerve damage · CNS toxicity · hypoglycemia · aortic aneurysm/dissection.

Other concerns

C. difficile · hepatotoxicity · QTc prolongation · CYP-related drug interactions · chelation · tube-feed complications.

Ozzy says: moxifloxacin is the odd FQ out here — no Pseudomonas and no urinary penetration.
Deck p. 15: The adverse-event slide separates black-box warnings, other adverse effects, and medication-related concerns such as chelation and tube-feed issues.
Why still use fluoroquinolones? The deck emphasizes high bioavailability, long half-life, low volume of distribution, and a favorable pharmacokinetic profile for sequential oral therapy.

Metronidazole

Passive diffusion → activation/reduction in bacterial cytoplasm → electron transfer to nitro group → DNA strand breakage.

Deck indications: anaerobes, bacterial vaginosis, protozoal infection, and C. difficile*. Adverse effects shown: peripheral neuropathy, gynecomastia, and a disulfiram-like reaction*.

Rifamycins

Inhibit DNA-dependent RNA polymerase → stop transcription.
Rifampin
Broad spectrum; do not use as monotherapy; often used for biofilm penetration.
Rifabutin
Primarily used for NTM; somewhat better drug-interaction profile.
Rifaximin
Poorly absorbed; GI use; deck lists hepatic encephalopathy.
Rifamycin pharmacology: CYP enzyme induction (rifampin > rifabutin), body-fluid discoloration, hepatotoxicity, flu-like symptoms. Rapid resistance is why rifampin is not used as monotherapy.

3. DNA-Precursor Inhibition: TMP-SMX

Sulfamethoxazole blocks DHPS + trimethoprim blocks DHFR → sequential folate-pathway inhibition → less tetrahydrofolate for purine/pyrimidine synthesis.
Deck p. 22: The folate-pathway diagram places sulfamethoxazole at DHPS and trimethoprim at DHFR.

Spectrum listed

Strep · Staph aureus · Enterobacterales · protozoa · Pneumocystis · Stenotrophomonas · Acinetobacter spp · Nocardia.

Toxicity / pharmacology

GI distress · rash → Stevens-Johnson syndrome · bone-marrow suppression · nephrotoxicity · avoid 1st/3rd trimester · high bioavailability · expected SCr bump · hyperkalemia · IV hyponatremia.

Deck p. 23: TMP-SMX summary integrates spectrum, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, marrow suppression, renal/electrolyte issues, pregnancy timing, and high oral bioavailability.

4. Ribosomal Protein Inhibitors

Protein-synthesis scaffold in the deck: 30S + 50S initiation → tRNAs add amino acids during elongation → stop codon triggers termination and polypeptide release.

Aminoglycosides · 30S

Bind 30S → mRNA misreading and defective cell membrane. Historical uses: double Gram-negative coverage and Gram-positive synergy; the deck says they have largely fallen out of favor.

DrugDeck spectrum / use clue
GentamicinEnterobacterales; no longer considered anti-Pseudomonal
TobramycinEnterobacterales + Pseudomonas; rising resistance
AmikacinEnterobacterales + Pseudomonas + NTM; deck notes Pseudomonas activity only in urine
Plazomicin*Enterobacterales; UTI only
Aminoglycoside toxicities: nephrotoxicity · neuromuscular blockade · ototoxicity · vertigo · avoid in pregnancy.

Tetracyclines · 30S

Prevent tRNA binding to the 30S ribosome during elongation.
Deck p. 30: Doxycycline is organized by spectrum, clinical use, pharmacology, and toxicity; the deck highlights MRSA, atypicals, rickettsial organisms, syphilis, chelation, photosensitivity, tooth discoloration, pill esophagitis, and pregnancy contraindication.

Doxycycline

MRSA Staph · atypicals · protozoa · rickettsiae · syphilis. Uses shown: SSTI/bone-joint infection, CAP, malaria prophylaxis, tick-borne illness, STIs. Poor urinary penetration.

Other tetracyclines*

Minocycline, tigecycline, eravacycline, omadacycline. The deck compares MDR Gram-negative / polymicrobial use, route, volume of distribution, GI toxicity, and mycobacterial coverage.

Macrolides · 50S

The deck states they inhibit transpeptidation in elongation by binding 50S. Spectrum emphasis: atypicals, NTM, and some STIs. Overuse has produced high resistance rates among Gram-positive organisms.

Azithromycin
Once daily · less potent CYP inhibitor · GI effects · QTc prolongation.
Clarithromycin
Twice daily · potent CYP inhibitor · more severe GI effects · more severe QTc prolongation.

Clindamycin · 50S

Binds 50S to prevent peptide-bond formation. Spectrum listed: Staph, Streptococcus, anaerobes except B. fragilis, Toxoplasmosis, Pneumocystis. Major deck signal: C. difficile + diarrhea; handout also notes anti-toxin effect in GAS necrotizing fasciitis.

Linezolid · 50S

Binds 50S to prevent translation. Spectrum: Staph, Strep, Enterococcus, Mycobacterium, Nocardia. Toxicities: thrombocytopenia, peripheral/optic neuropathy, lactic acidosis, serotonin syndrome, rhabdomyolysis.

Deck p. 37: The linezolid slide pairs Gram-positive/mycobacterial/Nocardia spectrum with timing clues: thrombocytopenia around 2 weeks and peripheral/optic neuropathy around 4 weeks.

5. Faculty Practice Questions

Q1. Which listed drug covers Gram-negative organisms?
Answer: Ceftriaxone.
Q2. Which drug needs weekly CPK monitoring?
Answer: Daptomycin.
Q3. Which drug should not be used alone because resistance develops rapidly?
Answer: Rifampin.
Q4. Which anti-MRSA drug binds D-Ala–D-Ala and inhibits trans-glycosidation?
Answer: Vancomycin.
Q5. Fever + loose stools + positive C. difficile after an antibiotic course; most likely listed culprit?
Answer: Clindamycin.

6. Final Integration

Deck p. 46: The final handout closes with three useful regimen buckets: anti-MRSA, anti-Pseudomonas, and anti-anaerobic therapies.

Anti-MRSA list in handout

Vancomycin · daptomycin · TMP-SMX · doxycycline · clindamycin · linezolid.

Anti-Pseudomonas list

Ciprofloxacin · levofloxacin · tobramycin · amikacin.

Anti-anaerobic list

Moxifloxacin · metronidazole · clindamycin.

Last 60 seconds: Vanc = D-Ala-D-Ala / Gram+ / nephro + infusion · Dapto = K+ depolarization / weekly CPK / no pneumonia · FQ = topo II/IV / tendon-neuro-QT-chelation · Flagyl = reduced nitro → DNA breaks · Rifampin = RNA polymerase / CYP inducer / never solo · TMP-SMX = DHPS + DHFR / SJS + hyperK · aminoglycosides + tetracyclines = 30S · macrolides + clinda + linezolid = 50S.
